summary.text: A cyclic permutation is a permutation consisting of a single cycle, and one with k elements may be called a k-cycle.
In cycle notation it is written as the list of its elements in parentheses, in the order each is permuted to the next.
Every permutation on finitely many elements can be split into cyclic permutations whose non-trivial orbits are disjoint.

facts.label: Other name
facts.value: Cyclic permutations are sometimes just called cycles

facts.label: Disputed definition
facts.value: Authors disagree on whether fixed points are allowed

facts.label: Fixed point
facts.value: The orbit of a 1-cycle is a fixed point

facts.label: Cycle type
facts.value: The multiset of cycle lengths is fixed by the permutation

items.prompt: A permutation is written (1 3 2 4) in cycle notation, with each element sent to the next one listed and the last sent back to the first. Where does 2 go?
items.explain: The cycle sends 1 to 3, 3 to 2, 2 to 4 and 4 back to 1.

items.prompt: A shuffle moves card a to b's spot, card b to c's spot, and card c to a's spot. How is it classed?
items.explain: A cycle with k elements is a k-cycle, and this one cycles three elements, so it is a 3-cycle.

items.prompt: A permutation swaps 1 with 2 and, separately, swaps 3 with 4. Into what cycles does it break?
items.explain: Each swap is a cycle of two elements, and the two cycles do not share elements, so the permutation is made of two 2-cycles.

items.prompt: Two textbooks disagree about whether (1 3 2)(4), which cycles three elements and leaves 4 alone, counts as a cyclic permutation. What are they disagreeing about?

options.label: Whether cycles may have three elements
Whether the numbers must be listed in increasing order
Whether a permutation can be written in cycle notation
Whether a cyclic permutation may leave some elements fixed

items.explain: There is no widespread consensus on the definition: some authors allow fixed points alongside one non-trivial cycle, and others do not.

items.prompt: A permutation of the elements 1, 2, 3 and 4 is written as just (1 3 2). What does the missing 4 mean?

options.label: The permutation is not defined on 4
4 is a fixed point, a 1-cycle left out of the notation
4 is sent to 1 to close the cycle

items.explain: When no confusion will result, 1-cycles are often omitted, and the orbit of a 1-cycle is a fixed point.

items.prompt: Two people each break the same permutation into cycles with no elements in common. Which statement is right?

options.label: They get the same cycles, possibly listed in a different order
They can get cycles of entirely different lengths
Only one of them can write it as such cycles
The cycles must come out in the same order

items.explain: Any permutation can be written as a product of disjoint cycles, unique up to the order of the factors, so the cycle lengths are determined by the permutation.

paragraphs.heading: One single cycle
paragraphs.text: In group theory, a cyclic permutation is a permutation made of just one cycle. Such permutations are sometimes simply called cycles, and one with k elements may be called a k-cycle. In cycle notation you write its elements inside parentheses, in the order each one is sent to the next. So (1 3 2 4) takes 1 to 3, then 3 to 2, then 2 to 4, and finally 4 back to 1, which makes it a 4-cycle.

paragraphs.heading: Two definitions
paragraphs.text: Mathematicians do not fully agree on the exact definition. Some ask for a single cycle and nothing else, while others also allow fixed points next to at most one non-trivial cycle. Under that wider reading, (1 3 2)(4), which takes 1 to 3, then 3 to 2, then 2 back to 1, and leaves 4 alone, counts as a 3-cycle for some authors. There, each fixed point forms a trivial orbit, and all the other points share a single non-trivial orbit, so a cyclic permutation is one with exactly one non-trivial orbit.

paragraphs.heading: Building blocks
paragraphs.text: Every permutation of finitely many elements can be split into cyclic permutations whose non-trivial orbits do not overlap. Such disjoint cycles commute with each other, and the split is unique apart from the order of the cycles. The multiset of cycle lengths, called the cycle type, is therefore fixed by the permutation. It in turn determines both the signature of the permutation and its conjugacy class in the symmetric group.

paragraphs.heading: Writing and reading cycles
paragraphs.text: A cycle is written compactly as σ = (s₀ s₁ … sₖ₋₁), with no commas, so it is not mistaken for a k-tuple. Its length is the number of elements in its largest orbit, and a cycle of length k is a k-cycle. The orbit of a 1-cycle is a fixed point, yet as a permutation every 1-cycle is the identity. In practice, 1-cycles are often left out of cycle notation when this causes no confusion.

paragraphs.heading: Undoing a cycle
paragraphs.text: To invert a cycle, reverse the order of its entries: the inverse of (s₀ s₁ … sₖ₋₁) is (sₖ₋₁ … s₁ s₀). Because (a b) = (b a), each two-cycle is its own inverse. And since disjoint cycles commute, you can invert a product of disjoint cycles by reversing each cycle on its own.

paragraphs.heading: Swaps and parity
paragraphs.text: A cycle with just two elements is called a transposition. The symmetric group is a Coxeter group, which means that elements of order 2, namely the adjacent transpositions, generate it. A central result says that every way of writing a given permutation as a product of transpositions uses either an even number of them every time, or an odd number every time. That is what makes the parity of a permutation a well-defined idea.
